slides.title: Chapter 15: Google Sheets
slides.say: This chapter of the book, Google Sheets, explains how a Python program reads and writes Google spreadsheets with the library EZSheets: signing in, spreadsheet objects, sheet objects, forms and quotas, and a project. Google was never reached while this deck was made: every result comes from the real library talking to a stand-in for Google's answers, and each result slide says so. The deck has twenty-five code examples that run on the chapter page, five true stories, and tables where a comparison helps. Slide 2 lays out the five parts. Chapter 14 comes before it with Excel spreadsheets.

slides.title: Today's route through five parts
slides.say: The table is the map of the chapter. Each row is one of the five parts, with the slides it covers, the number of code examples and what you will run in it. The last row covers the table of objects and requests, the changes against the book, the summary, the practice questions and the links. The same twenty-five examples are listed in the chapter-code tab of the page, in this order, so a slide and its tab can be opened side by side. Part 1 starts on slide 4, and each later part begins with a divider slide that names its four ideas.

slides.title: Two questions this chapter answers
slides.say: Two questions run through the chapter, and the deck answers them near the end. The first asks which object of EZSheets stands for which part of a Google account and which request each call sends; the answer is the table on slide 49. The second asks where the book's printed outputs, programs and files differ from today; slide 50 lists those changes from the chapter research. Keeping both questions in mind makes each later slide easier to place.

slides.title: Part 1: Access, sign-in and token files
slides.say: Part 1 is about access. Before any request leaves the program it must be let in: a cloud project, a credentials file, a sign-in and token files. The four cards are the ideas of the part: the credentials file, the token file, the scope and the refresh token. Slides 5 to 14 cover them, using the pieces that run without an account: the address of the sign-in, the challenge, the token as a pickle and its expiry. Part 2 later uses the signed-in library.

slides.title: In short: setting up the account
slides.say: Setting up has a fixed order: a project in the Google Cloud console, the Sheets and Drive APIs turned on in it, a consent screen that names the program and its permissions, and then a credentials file with a client id and secret. The rows give a plain meaning to each idea, from installing EZSheets with pip to the credentials file that names the program but holds no user token. Slide 6 continues with the sign-in that uses the credentials file, and slide 7 shows the library before any sign-in.

slides.title: In short: signing in and tokens
slides.say: A token is a saved permission with an expiry, and the refresh token asks for a new one without another sign-in. The rows explain the first login with the credentials file, ezsheets.init(), the token file, the refresh token, the scope, the revoking of the credentials file, the pickle format in which the token is saved, and the module that opens the browser page. Slide 8 shows what a token holds, slide 13 a pickle, and slide 14 the lifetime of a token.

slides.title: Before the sign-in: what EZSheets knows
slides.say: Before any sign-in the library already knows its release, 2026.4.28, and its two scopes: the whole spreadsheets scope and the whole drive scope. The flag IS_INITIALIZED stays False until a sign-in has worked. The call uninstall takes the stand-in for Google out, so the result shows the library as it is before any account is used. The scope is the permission from slide 6, and slide 8 looks at the file that stores a token.

slides.title: A token file holds a credentials object
slides.say: A token file holds a credentials object. The example makes one with made-up values and prints its fields: the access token, the refresh token, the address where tokens are renewed, the scopes, the universe domain and the account. EZSheets saves such an object with pickle in a file named token-sheets.pickle, and slide 13 shows what that format allows. The access token is short-lived and the refresh token renews it, as slide 14 shows.

slides.title: Story: OAuth began in 2006 to end password sharing
slides.say: OAuth began in November 2006 at a CitizenSpace OpenID meeting, where Blaine Cook, Chris Messina and others found that no open standard existed for sharing access without sharing a password. A specification was drafted in July 2007 and the IETF published RFC 6749 in October 2012. The photograph shows Blaine Cook. Your token files, slides 8 and 13, are the result, and slide 10 shows the address of a sign-in that uses it.

slides.title: The sign-in address: code, offline access and a challenge
slides.say: No network is used. The flow builds the address that the browser would open for the sign-in, and the example reads three parts of it: the response type code, access type offline, and the challenge method S256. The credentials file is shown as a dictionary with made-up values. The return address is localhost on port 8080. Slide 12 explains the hashed challenge, and slide 9 tells how OAuth began.

slides.title: In short: the libraries underneath
slides.say: EZSheets is a thin layer. The short calls such as getRow belong to EZSheets, while Google's client library builds each request and Google's authentication library runs the sign-in. The last rows name three standard modules that the chapter research lists: http.client for HTTP connections, shlex for splitting a command line, and sys for the words typed after the program's name. Slide 10 shows the sign-in address that the authentication library builds, and slide 45 uses sys.

slides.title: The challenge is a hash of a secret the program keeps
slides.say: The program makes a random secret, the verifier, and keeps it. Only the SHA-256 hash of the verifier, the challenge, goes into the sign-in address, and later the program shows the verifier so that Google can hash it again and compare. The example uses the verifier printed in RFC 7636, the standard behind the challenge, which is on the resources slide. Slide 10 shows where the challenge appears in the address.

slides.title: A token file is a pickle, and a pickle can run code
slides.say: A pickle can run code when it is loaded. The class in the example tells pickle to call print, so loading its 67 bytes prints a line; in an attack the call could be any code. EZSheets loads token-sheets.pickle when it is imported, so a token file from someone else is a program, not data. The same danger is described on the OWASP page on the resources slide, and slide 8 shows the token that such a file holds.

slides.title: A token has a lifetime; the refresh token renews it
slides.say: The library compares a token's expiry with the clock, in UTC without a time zone. A fresh token is valid; a stale one and one a week old are expired, and an expired token is renewed with the refresh token. In an app in Testing status the refresh token itself dies after seven days, which slide 50 lists among the changes. Slide 8 shows the fields of a token.

slides.title: Part 2: Spreadsheet objects
slides.say: Part 2 is about spreadsheet objects. A Spreadsheet object stands for one spreadsheet of the account, and each call that creates, opens, changes or deletes one is a request to Google. The four cards are the ideas of the part: the Spreadsheet itself, its attributes, the export with downloadAs and the Trash. Slides 16 to 23 cover them. Part 1 earlier explains the sign-in that every one of these calls depends on.

slides.title: In short: spreadsheet objects
slides.say: A Spreadsheet object stands for one spreadsheet of the account. The rows explain the objects, the call that creates or opens one, the three jobs of creating, uploading and listing, the two functions upload and listSpreadsheets, the attributes of which only the title can be changed, and refresh, which reads the spreadsheet again. Slide 17 creates and lists, slide 18 opens by id and by address, and slide 19 shows the attributes.

slides.title: Create a spreadsheet, list the spreadsheets of the account
slides.say: The stand-in plays Google. Spreadsheet() creates an untitled spreadsheet, createSpreadsheet gives one a title, and listSpreadsheets returns a dictionary from each id to its title. The recorder of the stand-in counted fourteen requests so far, among them the requests that make a spreadsheet and the listing; a real quota counts the same requests. Slide 30 compares request counts for writes, and slide 49 lists the request each call sends.

slides.title: Open a spreadsheet: id, address and getIdFromUrl
slides.say: A spreadsheet can be opened by its id or by its address, and both give the same title. getIdFromUrl cuts the id by position, so an address that ends right after the id loses its last character: SHEET12 instead of SHEET123. The public sheets of the book are replaced by a stand-in loaded under a made-up id. Slide 50 notes that the book's short links were answered with 403, so opening by id is safer.

slides.title: Spreadsheet attributes: title, sheetTitles, id and url
slides.say: A Spreadsheet has four attributes: the title, the sheet titles, the id and the address. Only the title can be set, and the new title is sent to Google at once. The other three are properties without a setter, so setting one raises an AttributeError, which the program catches and prints. Slide 17 creates the spreadsheet that these attributes describe.

slides.title: Story: Google Sheets began as a small web spreadsheet
slides.say: Google Sheets began as XL2Web, made by 2Web Technologies; Google bought it in 2006 and opened a limited test on 6 June 2006. The photograph shows Jonathan Rochelle. A spreadsheet in a browser is a service that a program calls, not a file, which is why every call on slides 17 to 23 is a request. Chapter 14 tells how the file-based spreadsheet began.

slides.title: In short: downloading and deleting
slides.say: Downloading asks Google to export a spreadsheet as a file, and delete moves a spreadsheet to the Trash first. The rows explain downloading and uploading, the Excel export, the five other formats, deleting, the delete call with its permanent option, and the Trash, where a deleted spreadsheet stays and is still listed. Slide 22 shows six downloads and slide 23 shows the two kinds of delete.

slides.title: Upload a file, download a spreadsheet in six formats
slides.say: Upload turns a file into a spreadsheet, here a small CSV file made in a temporary folder. Each downloadAs method exports the spreadsheet and saves a file with the title as its name, in which spaces become underscores. The HTML export is saved as a zip. The book prints a plainer name, which slide 50 lists among the differences. Slide 23 shows what delete does to such a spreadsheet.

slides.title: Delete moves a spreadsheet to the Trash
slides.say: delete() only moves the spreadsheet to the Trash: the request is a PATCH that sets trashed to True, and the spreadsheet is still listed. delete(permanent=True) sends a DELETE request, and only then does the list lose it. Check your own Trash before you trust a list. Slide 49 names the request of each call, and slide 17 shows the listing that this slide changes.

slides.title: Part 3: Sheet objects
slides.say: Part 3 is about sheet objects. A Sheet object stands for one tab of a spreadsheet: its cells, rows and columns. A sheet is read from a local copy and written with requests, so the number of requests is the number to watch. The four cards are the ideas of the part: A1 notation, getRow and getColumn, updateColumn and copyTo. Slides 25 to 35 cover them. Part 4 next shows why the number of requests matters.

slides.title: In short: sheets, cells and addresses
slides.say: A sheet is a grid in which every cell has a name such as B2, with the column letter first, and a pair of numbers that start at 1. The rows explain the Sheet object, reading and writing a cell, A1 notation, counting from 1, and the three helper functions that convert between names, numbers and letters. Slide 26 reads and writes cells, and slide 27 runs the helpers. Chapter 14 uses the same names for Excel cells.

slides.title: Read and write a cell: A1 notation and column, row
slides.say: A cell is read by name or by column and row, both counting from 1. Reading from a loaded sheet sent no request, and a write is one PUT whose input is typed as if by a person. The local copy shows the number 30 after the write until refresh() reads the text that Google holds. The book prints the text 30, which slide 50 lists. Slide 27 shows the conversion of names, and slide 30 counts requests.

slides.title: Addresses and column letters: convertAddress and friends
slides.say: These are plain functions that need no account. convertAddress turns a name into a column and row pair and back, so A2 is (1, 2) and the pair (2, 5) is B5. getColumnLetterOf and getColumnNumberOf convert between letters and numbers: 27 is AA, 999 is ALK and ZZZ is column 18278. Letters count like digits without a zero. Slide 26 uses the names, and chapter 14 has the same converters for Excel.

slides.title: In short: rows and columns
slides.say: A row or a column is read as a list of text and changed with one request. The rows explain the six calls: getRow, getRows and getColumn read, and updateRow, updateRows and updateColumn replace a whole line. Every value is text. Slide 29 runs the calls on a produce sheet, and slide 30 counts the requests: one request for a column against one for each cell.

slides.title: Rows and columns: get and update whole lines
slides.say: Rows and columns are lists of text, and every value is a string. getRow and getColumn read a line, and getColumn accepts a letter or a number. updateRow and updateColumn replace a whole line with one request. The example upper-cases the first column and replaces row 3. Slide 30 counts the requests of these updates, and slide 33 moves on to the sheets themselves.

slides.title: Cell by cell costs a request each; a column costs one
slides.say: Writing eight values cell by cell sent eight requests, and updateColumn sent all eight in one. Google limits requests, not values, so batching is the cure for a slow program and for a refused one. The limit is described on the usage-limits page of the resources slide, and slide 40 shows what the library does when a request is refused.

slides.title: Story: Google turned off the old Sheets API in 2021
slides.say: Google turned down Sheets API version 3 on 2 August 2021, and EZSheets speaks version 4. The picture is a screenshot of the Google Sheets add-ons page, not of the API itself. A library is only as stable as the service behind it, which is why slide 50 lists what changed since the book was written. Slide 30 counts the requests that EZSheets sends.

slides.title: In short: more sheets in a spreadsheet
slides.say: A spreadsheet holds several sheets, and each can be created, moved, copied, cleared or deleted. The rows explain the creating, moving and deleting of sheets, the Sheet call that returns nothing in the current library, createSheet, which returns the new sheet, the delete of a sheet, the copying to another spreadsheet and the clear call that keeps the size. Slide 33 shows the sheets, slide 34 the copy and clear, and slide 35 three surprises of the library.

slides.title: Create, move and delete the sheets of a spreadsheet
slides.say: Spreadsheet.Sheet() returns None in the current library, although the sheet Spam does appear in the sheet titles afterwards. createSheet returns the Sheet, and a second argument chooses its place. Setting index moves a sheet and delete() removes one; sheets are counted from 0. The book's listings print Sheet objects, which slide 50 lists as a difference. Slide 34 copies a sheet.

slides.title: Copy a sheet to another spreadsheet, and clear one
slides.say: copyTo adds a sheet named Copy of, then the old name, to another spreadsheet, and refresh() reads it. clear() empties every cell but keeps the size: the sheet still has two rows and three columns. A new spreadsheet starts with one sheet, so the copy is its second. Slide 33 shows creating and deleting sheets, and slide 35 shows three surprises of the library.

slides.title: Surprises: equal sheets, the in operator, an empty cell
slides.say: Three surprises of the library. Two sheets are equal when their sheet ids are equal, and the first sheet of every new spreadsheet has the id 0, so sheets of unrelated spreadsheets compare equal. The in operator searches the coordinates, not the values, so a name in a cell is not found. An empty cell is an empty string, never None. Slide 29 shows the lists of text that rows and columns return.

slides.title: Part 4: Forms and quotas
slides.say: Part 4 is about forms and quotas. A Google Form saves its answers as rows of a spreadsheet, which EZSheets reads like any other sheet. Google limits how many requests a project may send each minute, and the library waits and retries when a request is refused. The four cards are the ideas of the part. Slides 37 to 40 cover them, and part 3 earlier showed how to send fewer requests.

slides.title: In short: forms and quotas
slides.say: A Google Form saves its answers as rows of a spreadsheet, and Google limits how many requests a project may send each minute. The rows explain Google Forms, the reading of its data with EZSheets, working with quotas, the quota itself, the setting IGNORE_QUOTA that switches off only the library's own throttle, and the practice programs of the chapter. Slide 38 collects e-mail addresses and slide 40 shows the library waiting.

slides.title: Google Forms answers are rows: collect the e-mail addresses
slides.say: A form saves each answer as a row of a spreadsheet; the three answers here stand in for the response sheet of a real form. Column 3 holds the addresses, the first item is the heading and is cut off, and a set removes the address that answered twice. Slide 39 tells how Google Forms began, and slide 29 shows getColumn, which this program uses.

slides.title: Story: Google Forms arrived in 2008
slides.say: Google Forms was introduced in 2008; the pages we could open give the year, not the day. The picture is a web page with the Forms icon and a link to a form. A form is a front door that writes rows for your script, and slide 38 reads those rows. Slide 37 gives the plain meaning of Google Forms.

slides.title: Quota: the library waits 10 to 45 seconds and retries
slides.say: Google answers 429 when a project sends too many requests, and the library waits and retries. In the example the pauses are recorded instead of slept: nine tries, 220 seconds in all, then an HttpError is raised. IGNORE_QUOTA does not change this retry. The page on usage limits, on the resources slide, gives Google's own figures, and slide 30 shows how to send fewer requests.

slides.title: Part 5: Project 11, a fake blockchain
slides.say: Part 5 is Project 11, a spreadsheet that pretends to be a blockchain. The program audits the Boringcoin ledger, adds a transaction, meets a lost update when two programs write at once, and checks the totals of the practice sheet. The four cards are the ideas of the part. Slides 42 to 48 cover them. Chapter 14 earlier showed the same kind of project on Excel files, and part 3 explains the calls that the project uses.

slides.title: In short: the project
slides.say: Project 11 builds a ledger called Boringcoin on a shared sheet. Auditing means adding up what each row moves, and a sheet of transactions is easy to audit and just as easy to forge. The rows explain the project, the fake blockchain and the checking of a sheet against a rule. Slide 43 audits the ledger, slide 45 adds a transaction, and slide 47 tells the story of the real electronic cash that the project copies as a joke.

slides.title: Project 11, step 1: audit the Boringcoin ledger
slides.say: Step 1 of Project 11. PRE-MINE invents money and every other row moves it: the sender loses the amount and the recipient gains it. If the ledger is honest, the balances add up to what was created, here 1,500 Boringcoins. The real sheet is a grid of 1,000 rows; this one has four ledger rows. Slide 44 shows what happens on the real grid, and slide 47 tells the story that the project copies.

slides.title: The audit meets an empty row of the grid
slides.say: The real sheet is a grid of 1,000 rows, so getRows also returns the empty rows. One added row shows it: the audit sees three rows, and int of an empty string raises a ValueError, so the loop of step 1 stops. A guard for an empty first cell avoids it. Slide 43 shows the audit that this guard completes, and slide 29 shows getRows.

slides.title: Project 11, step 2: add one transaction
slides.say: Step 2 of Project 11. The program reads sender, recipient and amount from the command line, here set by hand. Adding a row changes the size of the sheet, which costs three requests, and each of the three cells costs one more: six requests for one transaction. A name with a space needs quotes on the command line, or sys.argv has four items. Slide 46 shows what two such programs do together.

slides.title: Two programs add a row: one transaction is lost
slides.say: Two programs each count the next row from their own copy of the sheet, so both write to row 3, and the second silently replaces the first. No error is raised, and after a refresh row 3 holds the second program's text. Nothing in the program guards against it. Slide 45 shows the single program that this slide runs twice, and slide 48 checks totals.

slides.title: Story: a 2008 message announced the cash Boringcoin copies
slides.say: On 31 October 2008 Satoshi Nakamoto announced the paper bitcoin.pdf to a cryptography mailing list. No photograph of the author exists, so the picture is the first page of the paper. A ledger of rows is easy to audit and easy to forge, which is what slides 43 to 46 show on a sheet. The paper is on the resources slide.

slides.title: Finding mistakes in a spreadsheet: quantity times price
slides.say: The practice program checks each total against quantity times price. The heading is row 1, so the data starts at row 2, and the row numbers that the program prints count the heading. One total is wrong in this stand-in: row 3 says 130, and 3 times 40 is 120. Slide 43 walks over the rows of a ledger in the same way. Slide 52 asks for a version that prints the correct total.

slides.title: Which EZSheets object sends which request
slides.say: The table sums up which EZSheets object stands for which part of the account and which request it sends. A Spreadsheet is one spreadsheet, a Sheet one tab, getRow and getColumn read a loaded sheet without a request, updateColumn writes a column with one request, a change of size costs three requests, delete moves to the Trash, downloadAsExcel exports a file, and the token file is a local pickle. The last column names the slide that shows each row in code. It answers the first question of slide 3.

slides.title: What differs from the book today
slides.say: The book's scripts and outputs differ from today's in places. The table lists each change, what it is now, and the slide with its example. Sheet() returns None, a write shows the number until a refresh, downloads get a longer name, the quota figures differ, a Testing app signs in again every seven days, token files are pickles, the consent screen has new pages, and Step 2 sends six requests. It answers the second question of slide 3.

slides.title: Summary
slides.say: Five ideas are worth keeping. A program must be let in with a cloud project, a credentials file and token files. A token file is a pickle, so never load one you did not make. A Spreadsheet object stands for one spreadsheet and a Sheet object for one tab, and each call is a request. Batch your writes, because Google limits requests, not values. A ledger of rows is easy to audit and just as easy to forge. The chart counts the code examples in each part of this deck. Slide 3 holds the two questions that these ideas answer, and slide 50 lists what differs from the book.

slides.title: Practice Questions
slides.say: Four drills and a program. The first uses the addresses of slide 27 for column 703 and the name ZZ. The second counts requests, as slide 30 does. The third is the lost update of slide 46. The program extends the Bean Count check of slide 48 to print the correct total. Try each on the chapter page, and write the answer in one sentence before you run it.

slides.title: Resources: where to go next
slides.say: Start with the book chapter and the EZSheets documentation, then Google's pages on limits, values and scopes, and the standards behind the sign-in: OAuth, and RFC 7636 for the challenge. The Python and OWASP pages explain the danger of pickle, gspread is the other library for Google Sheets, and the last link is the paper that Project 11 copies as a joke. Choose one link and read it before the next class. Slide 49 and slide 50 name the objects and the changes that most of these pages describe in full.
